3.note: Here, **sons** may mean “descendants,” since it would be unusual for Bela to have two sons named Gera, one named here and the other in verse 5. The term “sons” may similarly mean “descendants” in other places in this chapter.

The phrase **and Abihud** represents the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. Some scholars have suggested a slight change based on their belief that a consonant may understandably have been dropped in the process of copying from the text read aloud. This would yield the reading “even the father of Ehud.” This would make sense, since otherwise Ehud would be named in verse 6 without any prior introduction. It would also distinguish this **Gera** from the one in verse 5. Furthermore, according to Judges 3:15, the judge named Ehud was the son of a Benjaminite man named Gera. If there is a major Bible translation in your area and it follows this interpretation, you may wish to do the same in your translation. Alternate translation: [even the father of Ehud]

6.note: The author is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the pronoun **these** already expresses its meaning. He is doing that in order to contrast most of the **sons of Ehud** with another group of them, whom he calls **they** later in this verse and whom he identifies by name in the next verse. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [these, for their part, were heads of fathers]

The pronoun **they** in this instance refers to the men whom the author names in the next verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers without naming those men here. Alternate translation: [but some of their uncles exiled them]

7.note: Many interpreters believe that **Ahijah** and “Ahoah” are variants of the same name, since it occurs between the names Naaman and Gera here and in verses 4–5. However, we do not recommend that you use the name “Ahoah” in the text of your translation, since it does not appear here in any Hebrew manuscript or ancient version. You may wish to indicate this possibility in a footnote.

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he exiled them** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the personal role of **Gera** in leading this activity. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [Gera led the others in exiling them]

8.q: וְ⁠שַׁחֲרַ֗יִם הוֹלִיד֙ בִּ⁠שְׂדֵ֣ה מוֹאָ֔ב מִן־שִׁלְח֖⁠וֹ אֹתָ֑⁠ם חוּשִׁ֥ים וְ⁠אֶֽת־בַּעֲרָ֖א נָשָֽׁי⁠ו
8.note: The author is describing one event before describing another event that preceded it. If it would be helpful your language, you may wish to relate these events in the order in which they happened. Alternate translation: [And after he sent away his wives Hushim and Baara, Shaharaim fathered in the field of Moab]

The author seems to expect that readers will recognize that **Shaharaim** was one of the sons of Ehud. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. The UST models one way to do that.
The author is using the term **field** to describe the land or territory of Moab, since there was much fertile agricultural area in that land. Alternate translation: [in the land of Moab]

The author is using **sent them away** as a common expression of his culture to mean “divorced them.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly, as the UST does.

12.note: The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he built** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to specify that it was **Shemed** specifically who built these cities. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he was the one who built]
See how you translated the term “daughters” in 2:23. Alternate translation: [and its surrounding villages]

13.note: The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he built** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to specify that it was **Shemed** specifically who built these cities. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [they were the ones who made the dwellers of Gath flee]

This could mean: (1) that these Benjaminites defeated soldiers who had come into Israel from Gath and made them **flee** from the battlefield. Some interpreters suggest that this may be a reference to the events described in 7:21. Alternate translation: [they were the ones who defeated soldiers from Gath in a battle] or (2) that these Benjaminites at some point drove the inhabitants of Gath out of that city and settled there. This is less likely, as there is no description of this anywhere else in the Bible. Alternate translation: [they were the ones who forced the inhabitants of Gath to leave that city so they could settle there]

21.note: Many interpreters believe that **Shimei** and “Shema” (verse 13) are variants of the same name, since verses 14–21 in this genealogy seem to list the descendants of men named in verses 12 and 13. However, we do not recommend that you use the name “Shema” in the text of your translation, since it does not appear here in any Hebrew manuscript or ancient version. You may wish to indicate this possibility in a footnote.

27.note: Many interpreters believe that **Jeroham** and “Jeremoth” (verse 14) are variants of the same name, since verses 22–27 in this genealogy seem to list the descendants of two men who are named in verses 14. However, we do not recommend that you use the name “Jeremoth” in the text of your translation, since it does not appear here in any Hebrew manuscript or ancient version. You may wish to indicate this possibility in a footnote.

28.note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [These {were} heads of fathers according to their generations]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:7. Alternate translation: [as their genealogies record them]

29.note: The pronoun **they** refers to further descendants of Benjamin. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Some other Benjaminites dwelled in Gibeon]

Some manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation have the name “Jeiel” here. This is supported by the similar list in 9:35. If there is a major Bible translation in your area and it supplies this name, you may wish to do the same in your translation. Alternate translation: [Jeiel was the father of Gibeon]

See how you translated the term “father” in 4:3. It is unlikely that the term is literal here, since the next two verses list this man’s actual sons, starting with the firstborn. Alternate translation: [The founder of the Benjaminite community in Gibeon]

30.note: Some manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation add the name “Ner” here. This is supported by the similar list in 9:36 and the mention of Ner at the start of 8:33. If there is a major Bible translation in your area and it supplies this name, you may wish to do the same in your translation. Alternate translation: [and Baal and Ner]

32.q: וְ⁠אַף־הֵ֗מָּה נֶ֧גֶד אֲחֵי⁠הֶ֛ם יָשְׁב֥וּ בִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם עִם־אֲחֵי⁠הֶֽם
32.note: In its first occurrence, the term **brothers** refers to the clan of Jeiel. In its second occurrence, it refers to the broader clan of Elpaal (verses 12–28). It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The descendants of Mikloth lived in Jerusalem, as did most of the descendants of Elpaal, while the other descendants of Jeiel lived in Gibeon]

The pronoun **they** seems to refer to Mikloth and his descendants, who, unlike the rest of Jeiel’s descendants, moved to Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Mikloth]

40.note: It might seem that this expression contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. However, it may be natural in some languages to use a fuller expression to introduce these **sons of Ulam**. Alternate translation: [warriors of valor] or [men who were warriors of valor]
See how you translated the same expression in 5:18. Alternate translation: [skillful archers]
Your language may have its own term or expression for the relationship that the author describes as **sons of sons**. Alternate translation: [and multipliers of sons and grandsons]

Here the masculine terms **sons** and **sons of sons** have a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [and multipliers of children and grandchildren] or [and men who had very large families]
